title: Perform primary meat inspection incisions of horse and donkey

lessons.title: Equine slaughter and preparing for inspection
lessons.html:
Background

Horse and donkey meat is not widely eaten in South Africa, but equines are slaughtered at registered abattoirs for export markets and other approved uses. Where meat is intended for human consumption, it must be inspected under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and its regulations, and must meet the requirements of importing countries.

Special concerns with equines

  • Medicine residues: horses are often treated with medicines that are not permitted in food animals, or that need long withdrawal periods. Treatment records and owner declarations are therefore very important. Animals without acceptable records may not be accepted for human consumption.
  • Controlled and zoonotic diseases: glanders (a serious zoonosis), African horse sickness, equine infectious anaemia and others. Suspected cases must be reported immediately under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984.
  • Parasites: Trichinella testing of horse meat is required by some importing countries.
  • Welfare: working donkeys and horses may arrive thin, lame or with harness sores.

Preparing the station

  • Good lighting at head, pluck, viscera and carcass points.
  • Arrangement for splitting the head along the midline so that the nasal septum and nasal passages can be examined.
  • System for keeping all parts matched to the carcass number.
  • Sterilizer, hand-wash basin, two sharp knives, steel and hook; sample containers if testing is required.
  • Detention area, tags and condemned containers.

Planning

Check the ante-mortem findings and the treatment documents for each animal before slaughter. Note nasal discharge, skin nodules, coughing, fever or lameness.

lessons.title: Performing the incisions on horses and donkeys
lessons.html:
Routine examination

Follow the sequence and incisions in which you were trained and which the regulations prescribe. The main areas are:

Head

  • Observe the head, mouth and skin.
  • Incise the mandibular (submaxillary) lymph nodes and other head lymph nodes as prescribed. Look for enlargement and abscesses: strangles, a bacterial infection, causes abscesses in these nodes.
  • Split the head and examine the nasal septum and nasal passages for nodules, ulcers or scars that may indicate glanders. Any suspicion must be referred immediately.

Pluck

  • Observe and palpate the lungs; incise the bronchial and mediastinal lymph nodes. Look for nodules (possible glanders), pneumonia and abscesses.
  • Large amounts of frothy fluid in the airways and oedema of the lungs may indicate African horse sickness.
  • Examine the heart sac and heart; incise as prescribed.
  • Observe and palpate the liver and spleen; incise the portal lymph nodes as prescribed.

Carcass

  • Observe the whole carcass, including the pleura, peritoneum and kidneys.
  • In grey horses, look for melanomas: black tumours that are common under the tail, around the anus and in the lymph nodes and organs.
  • Look for harness sores, bruising, injection-site lesions, abscesses and oedema.
  • Equine fat is often yellow; distinguish normal fat colour from jaundice by checking connective tissue and the sclera.
  • Take muscle samples for laboratory testing where required.

Hygiene and safety

Sterilise after every carcass and after cutting a lesion. Glanders can infect people through broken skin and mucous membranes: wear PPE and report any suspicion without further cutting.

lessons.title: Completing the equine inspection
lessons.html:
Findings and actions

FindingAction
No abnormalities and acceptable treatment recordsContinue to marking, after test results where required
Localised harness sore or bruiseMark for trimming
Strangles abscess in head lymph nodesDetain; examine for spread; refer
Nodules or ulcers on the nasal septum or lungsStop, detain, report immediately: possible glanders
Lung oedema with frothy fluidDetain and report: possible African horse sickness
Multiple melanomas in organs and lymph nodesDetain and refer; usually total condemnation
Missing or unacceptable medicine recordsNot passed for human consumption; refer

Holding for results

Where Trichinella or residue testing is required, carcasses are held under control and released only when results are recorded.

Records

  • Animal identification, owner, origin and treatment documents.
  • Findings, trimming, condemnations and detentions.
  • Samples taken and results.
  • Notifications of suspected controlled diseases.

Welfare feedback

Findings such as harness sores, emaciation and old injuries on working donkeys and horses should be recorded and reported through the proper channel, as they may indicate offences under the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962.

Key points

  • Equine meat may only be passed when acceptable medicine treatment records exist.
  • Split the head and examine the nasal septum for signs of glanders.
  • Strangles causes abscesses in head lymph nodes.
  • Frothy fluid and lung oedema may indicate African horse sickness.
  • Check grey horses for melanomas.
  • Report suspected controlled diseases immediately.

quiz.question: Why must the head of a horse be split during inspection?

options.text: To examine the nasal septum for signs of glanders
To remove the brain for sale
To check the teeth for age only

quiz.question: Abscesses in the head lymph nodes of a horse are often caused by what?
Where are melanomas commonly found in grey horses?

options.text: Under the tail, around the anus and in lymph nodes

quiz.question: Why are treatment records especially important for horses?

options.text: Horses are often treated with medicines not permitted in food animals

quiz.question: Large amounts of frothy fluid in the airways may indicate which disease?
A horse carcass with no treatment records may be passed if it looks healthy.

Nodules in the lungs suggesting glanders
